title: Real-Time Streaming Protocol Version 2.0
summary: RTSP 2.0 is an application-layer protocol for setting up and controlling delivery of real-time data such as audio and video, from live feeds or stored clips. It is an extensible framework for controlled, on-demand delivery. This standards-track RFC obsoletes RTSP 1.0 from RFC 2326.

plainLanguage.summary: Like a remote control for a video stream: play, pause, and jump around, while the media itself comes from somewhere else.

questions: how does rtsp control streaming media
what is the default rtsp port
subtitle: A network remote control for streaming servers: set up a session, then play, pause, seek and tear down media that travels by other means.

tldr.problem: Audio and video servers need a standard way for a client to choose what to watch, agree how the media will be delivered, and then start, stop and reposition it, without the control protocol carrying the media itself.
tldr.mechanism: RTSP 2.0 is a text-based request and response protocol over TCP or TLS. A client describes, sets up and plays a session with methods such as DESCRIBE, SETUP, PLAY, PAUSE and TEARDOWN, while the media flows separately, typically as RTP.
tldr.outcome: It is a Standards Track replacement for RTSP 1.0 (RFC 2326) that is deliberately not backwards compatible, drops RECORD, ANNOUNCE and RTSP over UDP, and adds pipelining, IPv6 and server notifications.

today: RFC 7826 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2326 (RTSP 1.0). The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. NAT traversal for RTSP 2.0 is specified separately in RFC 7825.

sections.title: A Network Remote Control
sections.content:
RFC 7826 defines version 2.0 of the Real-Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP). It is an application-layer protocol for setting up and controlling the delivery of data with real-time properties, typically streaming media such as video on demand or live audio. The RFC sums it up as a "network remote control" for multimedia servers.

The protocol runs between clients and servers, and it also allows proxies in between. A client can ask a server for a description of the media, set up the delivery channels, then play, pause or stop. The media can have several audio and video streams, delivered as time-synchronized streams from server to client.

RTSP 2.0 replaces RTSP 1.0 from RFC 2326 and obsoletes it. It is based on 1.0 but is not backwards compatible other than in the basic version negotiation. The RFC says that anyone implementing RTSP for a new use case, with no installed RTSP 1.0, should implement only RTSP 2.0.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a big video library far away. RTSP is the remote control you use to pick a video and press play or pause. The video itself arrives some other way.

sections.title: How a Session Works
sections.content:
RTSP has three fundamental parts: session establishment, media delivery control, and an extensibility model. It is a bidirectional request and response protocol: clients send requests, but servers can also send requests to clients. Messages are plain text, with a possible binary message body, and are sent over a reliable transport. Clients and servers must implement TCP and TLS over TCP for this.

RTSP does not describe the media itself. A presentation description says how many streams there are, what URI controls each, which delivery protocol is used and how to decode the media. It can arrive out of band or in the response to a DESCRIBE request, and the RFC defines how to use SDP for this in Appendix D.

The client then sends SETUP with a Transport header listing acceptable delivery alternatives in priority order. The server picks one, creates an RTSP session, and returns a session identifier in the Session header. Further SETUP requests that name the same session add more streams to it. A session with several streams is an aggregated session controlled through one aggregate control URI, so one PLAY or PAUSE acts on audio and video together.

To save a round trip, the client can pipeline the requests that set up and start a session. A Pipelined-Requests header binds them together as if they carried the session identifier.

A session stays alive while the client shows liveness, by sending any request that carries the session, or by RTCP reports when RTP is used. The default session timeout is 60 seconds, and the server can set another value in the timeout parameter of the Session header.
sections.plainLanguage: First you look at the menu, then you tell the kitchen how you want the food delivered, and the kitchen gives you a ticket number. You show the ticket every so often so they know you are still there.

sections.title: Media Time and Media Properties
sections.content:
Positions in the media are given in the Range header, in one of three time formats. Normal Play Time (NPT) is the position relative to the start of the presentation, such as npt=123.45-125; the special value now means the current instant of a live event. SMPTE time codes give frame-level offsets from the start of the clip, and absolute time uses a UTC timestamp such as clock=19961108T143720.25Z-19961108T144725.25Z.

What a client can do depends on the media. The server describes the content in the Media-Properties header of the SETUP response using independent attributes:

  • Random access: Random-Access, Beginning-Only or No-Seeking.
  • Retention: Unlimited, Time-Limited or Time-Duration.
  • Content modifications: Immutable, Dynamic or Time-Progressing.
  • Scales: the list of supported scale factors.

Combined, they describe on-demand media, dynamic on-demand media (for example a playlist), live media, and live media with recording. Live media is not seekable, so a client plays npt=now-. For live content being recorded, the Media-Range header tells the client how much is currently available, and a server that keeps only a recent window moves the start of that window forward as time passes.

Two headers change the pace. Scale is the ratio of media time delivered per unit of playback time: 2.0 is fast forward, values between 0 and 1.0 are slow motion, negative values play backwards, and 0 is not allowed. Speed is the ratio of playback time delivered per unit of wallclock time, which lets a client fill its buffer faster than it plays.
sections.plainLanguage: Time on a video can be counted from the start, by frame number, or by the wall clock. The server also tells you if the show can be skipped around, like a movie, or if it is live, like a ball game where you can only watch what is happening now.

sections.title: Messages, Headers and URIs
sections.content:
RTSP is text-based, using UTF-8, with lines ended by CRLF. A request carries a method, the resource it acts on and the protocol version; a response carries the version, a status code and a reason phrase. Headers follow, then an empty line, then an optional message body. Unknown headers must be ignored by clients and servers, and proxies must forward them. A body requires a Content-Length header, and RTSP does not support HTTP chunked transfer coding.

RTSP 2.0 defines three URI schemes. With rtsp, commands go over a reliable transport and the default port is 554. With rtsps, the transport is TLS and the default port is 322. The rtspu scheme exists only to register the scheme that RTSP 1.0 defined, and a server must answer a request using it with 501 (Not Implemented). The RFC also notes an alternative registered port, 8554.

Every request carries a CSeq sequence number. It matches responses to requests, and proxies use it to multiplex several clients onto one connection. Extensions are handled through feature tags: Supported lists what a party can do, Require makes a request fail with 551 (Option Not Supported) if a feature is missing, and Unsupported lists what was missing. The tag play.basic stands for the whole minimal playback functionality of this specification.

A session identifier is a string of 8 to 128 characters that must be cryptographically random. The RFC recommends 128 bits of entropy.
sections.plainLanguage: RTSP messages are plain notes: a first line saying what you want, some labelled lines of details, and sometimes an attachment. Every note has a number so replies can be matched to questions.

sections.title: Connections, Timeouts and Overload
sections.content:
RTSP 2.0 runs only over TCP or TCP with TLS. RTSP 1.0 attempted an optional UDP mode but did not specify it well enough for interoperable implementations, so RTSP 2.0 drops it. A side effect is that RTSP requests must not be sent to multicast groups. Because the transport is reliable, RTSP messages must not be retransmitted at the RTSP level.

A server must handle both persistent connections, used for many exchanges, and transient connections, used for one. A persistent connection is recommended, partly because a server can only send requests to a client over a connection the client has opened. A server that tries to send a request with no such connection must discard it. An agent may use one connection for several sessions on the same server, but not more than one connection per session at a time.

The RFC gives concrete timers. A responder should answer within 5 seconds, or send a 100 Continue response and repeat it every 5 seconds. A requester should wait at least 10 seconds before concluding that no response is coming. A server should wait at least 10 seconds after answering the last session-level TEARDOWN before closing the connection, in case the client wants to set up a new session. For keep-alives, SET_PARAMETER without a body is the recommended method, and servers must support it.

When overloaded, servers answer 503 (Service Unavailable) and proxies answer 553 (Proxy Unavailable), with a Retry-After header. The RFC requires the delay to grow with load and to vary between clients so they do not all return at once. It also recommends no more than 10 outstanding requests per session.
sections.plainLanguage: RTSP talks over a phone line that stays open, so nothing gets lost on the way. If the other side is slow to answer, you say you are still working on it, and if they stay silent too long you hang up.

sections.title: The Methods
sections.content:
The methods are the buttons on the remote control. OPTIONS asks what an agent supports and works in both directions. DESCRIBE fetches the presentation description. SETUP creates a session or changes the transport parameters of a stream, and its response must carry the Accept-Ranges and Media-Properties headers, plus Media-Range for time-progressing media.

PLAY starts delivery. The server positions playback at the start of the requested Range, adjusted according to the Seek-Style header, and always includes a Range header in its response with the actual start. For RTP the RTP-Info header carries the synchronization data. A range outside the media gets 457 (Invalid Range). When a PLAY arrives while already playing, it now takes effect at once: a first range with an explicit start replaces the current play, while a range with an implicit start such as npt=-25 only moves the end point. In an aggregated session, PLAY must use the aggregate control URI, otherwise the answer is 460 (Only Aggregate Operation Allowed).

PAUSE halts delivery and the response reports what remains of the range. A later PLAY without a Range resumes from the pause point. When playback reaches the end, the session does not leave the Play state by itself; only PAUSE does that.

Servers can send requests too. PLAY_NOTIFY informs the client of events during play, with the reasons end-of-stream, media-properties-update and scale-change. REDIRECT tells a client to move to another server, with a required Terminate-Reason header and a Location header. A server with nowhere to redirect to uses TEARDOWN instead. GET_PARAMETER and SET_PARAMETER read and write parameters or are used as keep-alives.

A client TEARDOWN on the aggregate URI ends the session, and the response then has no Session header. A TEARDOWN on one media URI inside an aggregate, allowed only in the Ready state, removes just that stream.
sections.plainLanguage: Play starts the show, pause freezes it, and teardown puts it all away. The server can also tap you on the shoulder to say the show ended or that you need to move to a different room.

sections.title: Media Delivery and Interleaving
sections.content:
RTSP does not carry media in its basic form. The RFC specifies delivery with RTP over UDP, over TCP, or over the RTSP connection itself, and leaves room for other protocols to be added. Appendix C defines the combinations of RTP profiles and lower-layer transports and how the Transport header describes them, including the use of RTCP for feedback and as a keep-alive.

When a network blocks UDP, for example behind a NAT, media can be interleaved with RTSP messages on the same TCP connection. The RFC says this should generally be avoided unless necessary because it complicates both ends and brings head-of-line blocking. Each block starts with an ASCII dollar sign (36), a one-octet channel identifier and a two-octet length, followed by exactly one upper-layer data unit such as an RTP packet. The channel numbers come from the interleaved parameter of the Transport header. When RTCP is used, it goes on the next channel up, and both channels carry traffic in both directions.

The two-octet length means that blocks cannot exceed 65535 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the video comes by one road and the remote control signals by another. If the video road is blocked, the video can be put in little labelled envelopes and sent along the control road too.

sections.title: The Session State Machine
sections.content:
Appendix B gives an informative state machine for each session, best read as the server's state. There are three states. Init means no session exists, Ready means the session can start playing, and Play means media is flowing from server to client. A correct SETUP moves Init to Ready, PLAY moves Ready to Play, and PAUSE moves Play back to Ready. A TEARDOWN of the whole presentation, a session timeout, or an accepted REDIRECT without a deadline returns the session to Init.

The state machine deliberately avoids automatic transitions. When all media has finished playing, the session still stays in Play until the client sends PAUSE. In the Play state a SETUP for a new stream is refused with 455 (Method Not Valid in This State), and so is a TEARDOWN of a single media URI in an aggregate. A SETUP for an already set-up stream may change its transport parameters if the server implements that. The RFC says that where this appendix and the earlier sections disagree, the earlier sections win.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a video player with three modes: nothing loaded, loaded and waiting, and playing. Each button moves you from one mode to the next, and nothing changes mode by itself.

sections.title: Authentication, TLS and Threats
sections.content:
RTSP reuses HTTP security. Clients must implement both Basic and Digest authentication, and servers should. The RFC stresses that HTTP authentication alone does not give full message security, so TLS should be used, and a message with Basic credentials must travel over TLS with confidentiality. Agents must implement RTSP over TLS, signalled by the rtsps scheme. If a client tries rtsp where policy requires a secure channel, the server must redirect with 301 to an rtsps URI.

Proxies are a special case, since a proxy is a man in the middle. The client can send an Accept-Credentials header to tell proxies how to treat the next hop's certificate: Any, Proxy (the default) or User, where the proxy returns the certificate chain and the client decides. A proxy that cannot establish the next-hop TLS connection answers 472 (Failure to Establish Secure Connection).

The authentication mechanism only covers client-to-server requests. Server-to-client requests outside TLS are more exposed to message injection: REDIRECT to hijacking, TEARDOWN and PLAY_NOTIFY to denial of service.

The security considerations also cover session hijacking, mitigated by large, random, non-sequential session identifiers, and resource exhaustion by servers that hold state. A remote denial-of-service attack is possible because a client can name another address as the media destination in SETUP. A server must therefore only accept client-specified destinations once it has verified that the destination accepts the media. Media confidentiality and integrity are left to the media transport, and the RFC points to SRTP for RTP.
sections.plainLanguage: A password proves who you are, and TLS is a sealed envelope so nobody can read or change the messages. A careful server will not blast a video at a stranger's address just because you asked it to.

sections.title: What Changed from RTSP 1.0
sections.content:
The RFC lists what was removed: the RECORD and ANNOUNCE methods and everything tied to them, RTSP message transport over UDP, and the use of PLAY as a keep-alive in the Play state. It added server-to-client TEARDOWN, the asynchronous PLAY_NOTIFY, IPv6 support, extended IANA registries, request pipelining, a reworked state machine and an expanded REDIRECT. The text of the HTTP parts is now included in the document instead of being referenced.

Behavior also changed. In RFC 2326 a PLAY received in the Play state was queued until the current play finished; now it takes effect immediately. The Transport header gained src_addr and dest_addr, which replace the older port, client_port, server_port, destination and source parameters.

On compatibility, a server must answer RTSP/2.0 requests with RTSP/2.0, and it may answer an RTSP 1.0 request in kind if it chooses to support RFC 2326. Otherwise it must respond 505 (RTSP Version Not Supported). The RFC recommends against implementing RTSP 1.0 at all, since doing so interoperably is difficult.
sections.plainLanguage: The new version tidied up the old rulebook, dropped the parts nobody used, and made a few rules stricter. Because of that, old and new players cannot assume they understand each other and must check which version the other uses.
